title: Loud and soft
summary: Hear loud, soft and changing volume, then read the signs and Italian words that ask for it.

hook.text: Play a tune softly and it sounds like a lullaby. Play it loudly and it sounds like a march. Press play: this tune is played twice, and something changes. What do you hear? And what are those letters under the notes?

explore.text: Press play and listen: the tune goes quiet, then loud, then swells louder and louder. Play it again and hum along. Whisper the first [[bar|bar]], belt the second, and let your voice grow through the third.
explore.goal: Play the clip, then hum along: whisper, belt, then swell.

cards.text: Music has Italian words for volume. [[piano|Piano]] means quiet and is written *p*. [[forte|Forte]] means loud and is written *f*. They are the letters you saw. Press play: *p* in the first [[bar|bar]], then *f* in the second.

Add [[mezzo|mezzo]], which means medium, for [[mezzo-piano|mezzo piano]] (*mp*, fairly quiet) and [[mezzo-forte|mezzo forte]] (*mf*, fairly loud). Double a letter for the extremes: [[pianissimo|pianissimo]] (*pp*) and [[fortissimo|fortissimo]] (*ff*). Press play to climb all six steps.

A gradual change is drawn as a [[hairpin|hairpin]]: a long thin wedge under the notes. Opening out means getting louder: [[crescendo|crescendo]]. Closing in means getting quieter: [[diminuendo|diminuendo]], also called [[decrescendo|decrescendo]]. The words *cresc.* and *dim.* say the same.

alternative.text: Picture a storm. Far away, a faint rumble: *pp*. It comes closer, getting louder: a [[crescendo|crescendo]], written *cresc.* Overhead it roars: *ff*. Then it drifts off and fades: a [[diminuendo|diminuendo]], written *dim.* Press play and follow the words.

questions.prompt: Listen to both clips. Which one is played **forte**?
questions.hint: Forte is the loud one. Play both and ask which sounds played with more force.

options.reason: Clip B is played quietly, which is [[piano|piano]]. [[forte|Forte]] is loud, and that is clip A.

questions.hint: Compare the start of each clip with its end. Which one ends louder than it began?

options.reason: Clip A starts loud and fades away: that is getting quieter, a [[diminuendo|diminuendo]]. The clip that grows is clip B, a [[crescendo|crescendo]].

questions.prompt: Which sign tells you to get gradually **quieter**?
questions.hint: The wide end of a wedge is the loud end. Where should the wide end be if the sound is fading?

options.reason: That wedge opens out to the right, so it asks for the sound to grow: a [[crescendo|crescendo]]. Getting quieter needs a wedge that closes in.
*f* is [[forte|forte]]: loud, at one fixed level. A gradual change to quieter is drawn as a wedge that closes in.

questions.prompt: Match each sign to what it asks for.
questions.hint: Read the letters first: *pp* has two quiet letters. Then think about which way each wedge opens.

left.reason: *mf* is [[mezzo-forte|mezzo forte]]. The *m* is for [[mezzo|mezzo]], so it is fairly loud, not very loud.
A wedge that opens out is a [[crescendo|crescendo]]: the sound grows.
A wedge that closes in is a [[diminuendo|diminuendo]]: the sound fades.

questions.prompt: Put these signs in order, from quietest to loudest.
questions.hint: More *p*s means quieter and more *f*s means louder. Find the quietest one first.

payload.reason: Quietest to loudest: *pp* very quiet, *p* quiet, *mf* fairly loud, *f* loud, *ff* very loud.

questions.prompt: Listen to both clips. Which one is **piano**?
questions.hint: Piano is the quiet one. Which clip sounds hushed?

options.reason: Clip A is played loudly, which is [[forte|forte]]. [[piano|Piano]] is quiet, and that is clip B.

questions.prompt: What happens to the volume in this clip?
questions.hint: Listen to the first [[bar|bar]], then the last. Is the end louder, quieter or the same?

options.reason: The clip begins loud and ends soft, so it fades. Getting louder would be a [[crescendo|crescendo]].
The volume does not stay put: the clip starts loud and ends soft. One steady level would be a single sign such as *f*.

questions.prompt: Which sign matches what you hear?
questions.hint: Is the clip growing or fading? Then ask which way the wedge should open.

options.reason: That wedge closes in, which asks for fading: a [[diminuendo|diminuendo]]. The clip grows louder, so it needs a wedge that opens out.
*p* is one quiet level. The clip changes from quiet to loud, which is drawn as a wedge, not a single letter.

questions.prompt: What does the sign under the first note mean?
questions.hint: The *m* is for mezzo. The *f* says which side of the middle you are on.

options.reason: Fairly quiet is *mp*. The *f* in *mf* means loud, so this sign is fairly loud.
Very loud is *ff*. *mf* has an *m* for [[mezzo|mezzo]], so it sits nearer the middle: fairly loud.

questions.prompt: Put all six signs in order, from quietest to loudest.
questions.hint: Sort the *p*s and the *f*s first. The *m* signs sit in the middle.

payload.reason: Quietest to loudest: *pp*, *p*, *mp*, *mf*, *f*, *ff*. The *m* signs sit between the *p*s and the *f*s.

questions.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.hint: Words that end in -issimo are extreme. Mezzo means half.

left.reason: A [[crescendo|crescendo]] is a change: the sound gets gradually louder.
A [[diminuendo|diminuendo]] fades: the sound gets gradually quieter.
[[mezzo-piano|Mezzo piano]] is *mp*: halfway to quiet, so fairly quiet.

questions.prompt: Play the clip. One [[bar|bar]] has a sign that does not match what you hear. Tap that [[bar|bar]].
questions.hint: Listen to the third [[bar|bar]] of the clip. Is the sound growing or fading there?

payload.explanation: [[bar|Bar]] 3 has a wedge that opens out, asking for louder, but the music fades there. It needs a wedge that closes in: a [[diminuendo|diminuendo]].

questions.hint: Doubling a letter makes the idea stronger. Which letter means loud?

options.reason: *pp* is [[pianissimo|pianissimo]]: very quiet. Very loud has two *f*s.
*f* is [[forte|forte]]: loud, but not very loud. Doubling the letter makes it very loud.

questions.prompt: Which pair of words means the same thing?
questions.hint: One word gradually gets quieter. Which other word does that too?

options.reason: These are opposites: [[crescendo|crescendo]] gets louder and [[diminuendo|diminuendo]] gets quieter.
[[piano|Piano]] is quiet and [[pianissimo|pianissimo]] is very quiet. They are close, but not the same.

points: *p* means quiet and *f* means loud. Put an *m* in front for fairly: *mp* is fairly quiet and *mf* is fairly loud.
Doubling a letter goes to the extreme. Quietest to loudest: *pp*, *p*, *mp*, *mf*, *f*, *ff*.
A hairpin that opens out is a crescendo: gradually louder. One that closes in is a diminuendo, or decrescendo: gradually quieter.
The words *cresc.* and *dim.* mean the same as the hairpins.
